summary: D287 has no exam: you pass one performance assessment by customizing a provided Spring Boot MVC inventory web app (Thymeleaf pages over an H2 database) for a shop of your choice and adding features step by step, from new pages and sample data to new fields with validation messages. You work in a WGU GitLab repository, commit and push after each task, and note your changes in the README. It's 3 CUs in term 5 of the BSCS standard path; the instructors' webinar videos cover most steps, but 2026 reports say the project changed and some walkthroughs no longer match every requirement.
author: Dorian Acosta

assessment.type: Performance assessment: customize a Spring Boot inventory web app in GitLab
assessment.format: One project · a series of code tasks in a WGU GitLab repository · commit and push after each · evaluator-graded against a rubric, no exam
details: The app: a provided Spring Boot MVC project that tracks a shop's parts and the products built from them. It has JPA entities, Spring Data repositories, services, validators with custom annotations, controllers and Thymeleaf templates over an H2 database, plus a startup class for sample data (BootStrapData), application.properties, tests, pom.xml and a README. You pick the kind of shop.

The task in general terms (your task page has the exact requirements): you customize the app for your shop and extend it in small steps, such as unit tests, new pages, sample data loaded at startup, a purchase action and new fields with validation messages. Each step touches a few of the MVC pieces: controllers, Thymeleaf templates, entities, repositories, validators or tests.
Workflow: clone the WGU GitLab repository into your IDE and work on a branch. After each task, commit with a message and push, and note the change in README.md the way your task page asks.
Grading: evaluators grade the project against the task's rubric, and your commits and their messages are part of what they see. Your task page lists exactly what to submit.

Version change (reported): a Feb 2026 student found that the walkthrough videos skip some tasks, that one demo shows only part of its task, and that the completed-project demo and user guide show features that don't match the current tasks. An Apr 2026 commenter heard the project had changed. Follow your current task page and rubric over any guide, this one included.

Course facts: 3 CUs (course number ITSW 3173) in term 5 of the BSCS standard path, catalog 202611, alongside D286 Java Fundamentals, and WGU expects OOP and Java basics first. D288 Back-End Programming (term 6 in the November 2026 catalog; the June 2026 program guidebook lists it in term 8) and D387 Advanced Java come later, and Version Control (D197) in term 3 practices the same Git and GitLab basics.
tips: Turn every bullet on the task page into a checklist line and test each one in the running app before you submit; a single task can list several separate requirements.
Commit and push right after each task with a message that names it, so your history shows one step per requirement.
Write each README entry as soon as you make the change, while the details are fresh; your task page says what each entry needs.

Watch the instructors' webinar walkthroughs (course page → Course Community → Join WGU Connect → Resources). Students report they skip some tasks, and a Feb 2026 student found a demo that shows only part of its task, so check each video against your current task page.
Extend the provided design instead of rewriting it: keep the Part class abstract (commenters stress this), keep its inheritance mapping, and add new fields alongside the existing ones.
Pointing application.properties at a new database file starts a fresh, empty database, so your sample-data code runs again; use that to test your seeding guard.
Test each new action for side effects. Commenters point out that adding or updating a product can lower part inventory, so check that a purchase changes only what your task page says it should.
When the app won't start or a page shows a Whitelabel error, scroll the console to the last 'Caused by' line; it usually names a mapping, template or property mistake.

competencies: Course planning: discuss your course planning tool report with your instructor and create your personalized course plan together (listed first in the program guide).
The learner implements object-oriented programming frameworks.

topics.title: The project at a glance
topics.eli5: You're handed a working inventory app and asked to remodel it for your own shop, one small, checkable change at a time.
topics.detail: The provided project is a Spring Boot web app that tracks parts and the products assembled from them: users list, add, update and delete parts and products through Thymeleaf forms, and the data lives in an H2 database file. The code follows model-view-controller (MVC): entity classes describe the data, repository interfaces read and write it, service classes hold the logic, controllers map URLs to methods, templates render the pages, validators enforce rules through custom annotations, and a startup class (BootStrapData) can load sample data. Parts come in more than one concrete type, which is why the base Part class is abstract. Before you change anything, run the app, click through every page, and trace one request, such as adding a part, from the form through the controller, service and repository and back to a template, so you know where each requirement's change belongs.
points: Typical layout: domain (entities), repositories, service, controllers, validators, bootstrap, resources/templates (HTML), resources/static (CSS), application.properties, the test folder, pom.xml and README.md
Start the app from the main class annotated @SpringBootApplication, then open localhost:8080
Plan your shop's sample parts and products on paper first, including which parts go into which products
Change only what a requirement asks for; unrelated refactoring makes your README and commits harder to follow

topics.title: Spring Boot essentials
topics.eli5: Spring Boot is a kit that wires an app together for you: it starts a web server, connects the database and finds your classes by their labels (annotations), so you mostly write the parts that are unique to your app.
topics.detail: @SpringBootApplication on the main class combines @SpringBootConfiguration, @EnableAutoConfiguration (configure beans based on what's on the classpath) and @ComponentScan (find classes marked @Component, @Service, @Repository or @Controller in the main class's package and below). Spring creates one managed object, a bean, for each of those classes and hands them to the classes that need them through a constructor or @Autowired, which is called dependency injection. Starters in pom.xml bring in groups of libraries (web, Thymeleaf, data JPA, validation, test), and Maven downloads them, builds the project and runs the tests, either from the IDE or with ./mvnw spring-boot:run and ./mvnw test when the project includes the Maven wrapper. Settings live in src/main/resources/application.properties, and the embedded web server listens on port 8080 unless server.port says otherwise.
points: A class outside the main class's package tree isn't scanned, so its @Controller never answers
Prefer constructor injection; a class with a single constructor needs no @Autowired
Never create a service or other Spring-managed class with new: Spring doesn't inject its dependencies, which stay null
Spring Boot 3 and later use jakarta.* imports and need Java 17 or newer, while Spring Boot 2 used javax.*; match what your pom.xml and existing imports use

topics.title: Controllers and request mapping
topics.eli5: A controller is the app's receptionist: when the browser asks for a web address, it decides which method handles the request and which page to send back.
topics.detail: A class annotated @Controller holds handler methods. @GetMapping("/about") maps GET requests for /about to a method and @PostMapping maps form submissions; both are shortcuts for @RequestMapping with an HTTP method. A handler in a @Controller usually returns a view name such as "about", which Thymeleaf renders from templates/about.html, while a @RestController returns data such as JSON instead of a page. Handler parameters supply what you need: a Model to pass data to the template (model.addAttribute("products", list)), @RequestParam for a query-string or form parameter, @PathVariable for a value inside the URL path, and @ModelAttribute to bind a whole form to an object. Returning "redirect:/path" sends the browser to another URL, and redirecting after a successful POST (Post/Redirect/Get) keeps a page refresh from repeating the action.
points: GET for pages and reads; POST for anything that changes data, such as a purchase, a save or a delete
A new page needs a route, a template and links in both directions
@RequestParam("id") Long id reads ?id=3 or a form field named id
Pass a result message through the Model when you render a page, or through RedirectAttributes flash attributes when you redirect
A Whitelabel page with status 404 means no handler matched the URL; 500 means a handler or template threw an exception

topics.title: Thymeleaf templates and static files
topics.eli5: A Thymeleaf template is an HTML page with fill-in-the-blank spots: the controller hands over the data, and Thymeleaf fills the blanks before the browser sees the page.
topics.detail: Templates live in src/main/resources/templates and CSS, images and scripts in src/main/resources/static. Thymeleaf attributes start with th:: th:text="${product.name}" replaces an element's text, th:each="p : ${products}" repeats an element for every item in a list, th:if and th:unless show or hide an element, and th:href="@{/about}" and th:action="@{/save}" build context-relative links and form targets, with parameters written as @{/edit(id=${p.id})}. In a form, th:object="${part}" names the object being edited and each th:field="*{name}" writes the input's id, name and current value, so the submitted value binds back to the same property. ${#fields.hasErrors('price')} tests a field for validation errors and th:errors="*{price}" prints its messages. A template mistake shows up only when that page renders, so open every page you touch after each change.
points: ${...} reads model attributes, and *{...} reads properties of the form's th:object
th:each="p, stat : ${list}" adds a status variable: stat.index counts from 0 and stat.count from 1, plus first and last (unnamed, it's called pStat)
Fixed text such as your shop's name can go straight into the HTML; data should come from the model
A button that changes data belongs in a form that submits with POST, not in a plain link

topics.title: JPA entities, inheritance and relationships
topics.eli5: An entity is a Java class whose objects are saved as rows in a database table, and its annotations are sticky labels telling the database layer which field is the ID and how the classes connect.
topics.detail: @Entity marks a class whose objects persist as table rows, @Id marks the primary key and @GeneratedValue lets the database assign it. An entity needs a public or protected no-argument constructor and can't be final, and an abstract class can still be an entity: it's never instantiated itself, but a query on it returns all of its subclasses. @Inheritance on the root class chooses how a hierarchy maps to tables: SINGLE_TABLE, the default, stores every subclass in one table with a discriminator column (@DiscriminatorColumn, @DiscriminatorValue), JOINED gives each subclass its own table joined by key, and TABLE_PER_CLASS gives each concrete class a complete table. Relationships use @ManyToMany, @OneToMany and @ManyToOne. In a bidirectional relationship the side without mappedBy is the owner, whose changes are written to the database (for many-to-many, to the join table), and the side with mappedBy is the inverse. A new field on an entity becomes a new column, which Hibernate adds for you when the schema setting allows it.
points: Adding a field means the field, its getter and setter, any constructor that should set it, and the sample data that uses it
Keep Part abstract, as commenters stress; the app creates and saves its subclasses
A Set relies on equals and hashCode, so two objects that compare equal count once; check how the provided classes define equality before adding look-alike items
Update a bidirectional relationship on the owning side, and keep both sides in sync in memory

topics.title: Repositories, services and Optional
topics.eli5: A repository is a librarian for one kind of record: ask it to save, find, count or delete, and it writes the database queries for you.
topics.detail: Declaring interface PartRepository extends CrudRepository<Part, Long> is enough for Spring Data to generate an implementation at startup. CrudRepository gives you save (insert or update; keep using the object it returns), saveAll, findById (which returns an Optional), existsById, findAll (an Iterable), count, delete, deleteById and deleteAll, and method names such as findByName(String name) turn into queries automatically. A @Service class wraps repositories with business rules so controllers stay thin, and Spring injects repositories into services and services into controllers. Because findById returns an Optional, decide what absence means with isPresent(), orElse(...) or orElseThrow() instead of assuming the record exists.
points: repository.count() == 0 is the simplest test for an empty table
Calling save on an object that already has an ID updates that row instead of inserting a new one
Keep each business rule in one place, usually a service or a validator, instead of copying it into several controllers
ListCrudRepository (Spring Data 3.0 and later, so Spring Boot 3+ projects only) offers the same methods but returns List where CrudRepository returns Iterable

topics.title: Seeding sample data at startup
topics.eli5: Seeding is stocking the shelves before the store opens: a startup helper checks whether the shelves are empty and only then puts out the starter stock.
topics.detail: A @Component class that implements CommandLineRunner has its run(String... args) method called once the application context has started, just before startup finishes, which makes it the usual place for sample data. Inject the repositories, build entity objects with constructors or setters, and save them; when samples refer to each other, save the referenced objects first. Guard the whole block with a check that both tables are empty, so restarting the app neither duplicates the samples nor overwrites a user's edits. With a file-based H2 database the data survives restarts (unless ddl-auto is create or create-drop), so test the guard by restarting twice and by pointing the app at a new database file, which should seed exactly once.
points: Check both repositories, not just one, before inserting anything
Give the samples realistic names, prices and inventory values for your shop, and fill in any fields you add later
Log a short line when seeding runs so the console shows whether it ran
Restart the app twice: the second start should add nothing

topics.title: Bean Validation and custom constraints
topics.eli5: Validation is a bouncer for your data: each rule is a check at the door, and when a check fails the bouncer hands back a note saying why.
topics.detail: Jakarta Bean Validation puts rules on fields as annotations such as @NotNull, @Size(min = 2, max = 30), @Min(0) and @Max(100). In a controller, mark the form object @Valid and put a BindingResult parameter immediately after it; if bindingResult.hasErrors() is true, return the form view so Thymeleaf can show the messages, and otherwise save and redirect. Without a BindingResult right after the validated parameter, a failed validation becomes an exception (a 400 error by default) instead of messages on the form. A custom constraint is an annotation marked @Constraint(validatedBy = MyValidator.class) with @Target, @Retention(RUNTIME) and the required message, groups and payload elements, paired with a class implementing ConstraintValidator<MyAnnotation, T> whose isValid returns false to reject a value. A rule that compares several fields of one object, such as stock that must sit between a minimum and a maximum, belongs in a class-level constraint (@Target(ElementType.TYPE)) whose validator receives the whole object, and its ConstraintValidatorContext can swap the default message for a more specific one.
points: By convention a validator treats null as valid and leaves null checks to @NotNull
bindingResult.rejectValue("field", "code", "message") adds an error yourself when a rule is checked in a controller or service
Good messages name the problem and the limit, such as "Quantity must be at least 1"

A class-level constraint's message is a global error, not a field error, so th:errors="*{stock}" won't show it; display it with th:errors="*{global}" (or list every error with ${#fields.allErrors()}), or attach it to a field in the validator by calling context.disableDefaultConstraintViolation() and then context.buildConstraintViolationWithTemplate(msg).addPropertyNode("stock").addConstraintViolation()
Test every path: below the minimum, above the maximum, and exactly at each limit, which should pass
Before deleting a validator class, search the project for its annotation so nothing still refers to it

topics.title: H2 and application.properties
topics.eli5: H2 is a small database that can live in a single file next to your project, and application.properties is the settings card that tells Spring Boot where that file is.
topics.detail: Spring Boot reads src/main/resources/application.properties at startup. spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:file:./shopdb (or jdbc:h2:~/shopdb for your home folder) points the app at an H2 database that runs inside the app and is stored in a file with the .mv.db extension, while jdbc:h2:mem:shopdb keeps an in-memory database that disappears when the app stops. Connecting to a file that doesn't exist yet creates a new, empty database, so changing the file name in the URL gives you a clean slate and runs your seeding code again. spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto controls the schema: update adds missing tables and columns, create rebuilds them at startup, create-drop also drops them at shutdown, and validate and none leave the schema alone. If the property isn't set, Spring Boot 2.4 and later use create-drop only for an in-memory URL (jdbc:h2:mem:) when no migration tool such as Flyway is present, and none for everything else, including a file-based H2 URL, so make sure your project sets it (update keeps your rows and adds new columns). If the project enables it (spring.h2.console.enabled=true), the H2 console at /h2-console lets you browse the tables during development.
points: Changing the URL's file name creates a new file; the old database file stays on disk
Stop the app before deleting or renaming a database file by hand
Property keys must be spelled exactly; Spring Boot ignores keys it doesn't recognize, so a typo silently keeps the default
One key=value setting per line, and # starts a comment

topics.title: Unit testing with JUnit
topics.eli5: A unit test is a tiny robot that checks one promise your code makes, such as 'after setting the minimum to 5, the getter returns 5', and raises an alarm when the promise breaks.
topics.detail: JUnit Jupiter tests are methods annotated @Test in classes under src/test/java, and @BeforeEach methods run before every test to build fresh objects so tests don't affect each other. Assertions come from org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions: assertEquals(expected, actual) (expected first, with a third delta argument for doubles), assertTrue, assertFalse, assertNotNull and assertThrows. A good unit test arranges an object, acts once and asserts the result; for a new field, check that the setter stores a value and the getter returns it, using a value other than the field's default so the test can tell 'stored' from 'never set'. Run tests from the IDE's gutter icons or Maven's test phase, and note that @SpringBootTest starts the whole application, which plain getter and setter tests don't need.
points: Follow the style of the tests already in the test class you're adding to
Swapping expected and actual still passes or fails the same way, but the failure message becomes misleading
A test with no assertion passes as long as nothing throws
Run the whole test class before committing; a test that doesn't compile breaks the build

topics.title: Git and GitLab workflow
topics.eli5: Git is a save-game history for your code: each commit is a labeled save point, a branch is a separate save slot, and pushing uploads your saves to GitLab, where the evaluator can see them.
topics.detail: Clone the WGU-provided repository (git clone with its URL, or the IDE's Get from VCS), then create and switch to a working branch with git switch -c working-branch (the older form is git checkout -b working-branch). For each task, stage the changed files (git add), commit with a message naming the task (git commit -m "Add About page") and push; the first push of a new branch uses git push -u origin working-branch to set its upstream, after which a plain git push works. git status shows what's staged, git log --oneline --graph --all draws the history in the terminal, and in GitLab, Code → Repository graph shows the branch history. Commit source files rather than build output or IDE settings, and push after every task so the history shows one step per requirement.
points: One task, one commit (or a few), each pushed, so the history shows your work step by step
Write messages a stranger could match to the rubric: name the task and what changed
If a push is rejected, run git pull first, resolve any conflict, then push again
Version Control (D197), earlier in the path, practices the same Git and GitLab basics

topics.title: Exceptions and error pages
topics.eli5: An exception is the program raising its hand to say something went wrong, and you can answer politely with a message on the page instead of letting the whole page crash.
topics.detail: Java exceptions are objects thrown with throw and handled with try/catch, with finally for cleanup that must always run. Checked exceptions such as IOException must be caught or declared with throws, while unchecked ones (RuntimeException and subclasses such as IllegalArgumentException, NullPointerException and NoSuchElementException) needn't be. Catch the most specific type you can handle, and never swallow an exception with an empty catch block. In Spring MVC, an exception that escapes a handler produces an error page (Spring Boot's Whitelabel page with status 500 by default), so for expected problems, such as a purchase when stock is zero, check the condition and show a message rather than letting something throw; an @ExceptionHandler method can also turn a specific exception into a friendlier page. When the app fails to start, read the console's last 'Caused by' line first, since it names the real problem, such as a missing bean, a bad mapping or an invalid property value, like a malformed datasource URL (a misspelled property key is silently ignored instead).
points: Optional.orElseThrow() throws NoSuchElementException when the value is missing
Validation failures aren't exceptions when a BindingResult follows @Valid; without one they become a 400 error
TemplateInputException usually means a misspelled view name or a Thymeleaf syntax error in that page
Read a stack trace from the top for what failed and from the 'Caused by' lines for why

practice.q: A handler in a class annotated @Controller is mapped with @GetMapping("/about") and returns the string "about". In a Spring Boot project that uses Thymeleaf, what does the browser receive?
choices: The word about, sent as the whole response body
The page rendered from src/main/resources/templates/about.html
A redirect to /about.html
The file src/main/resources/static/about, served as is
practice.why: In a @Controller, a returned String is a view name. Thymeleaf resolves it to templates/about.html, renders it with the model and sends the HTML. Sending the word itself as the body is what a @RestController (or @ResponseBody) does. A redirect needs the redirect: prefix, and files in static/ are served directly by URL without any controller.

practice.q: A button on a list page should change data on the server, for example by recording a purchase. Which design fits Spring MVC conventions?
choices: A plain link to a @GetMapping handler, because links are simpler
A @RestController that returns the updated list as JSON
A form that submits with GET to a @PostMapping handler
A form that submits with POST to a @PostMapping handler
practice.answer: A form that submits with POST to a @PostMapping handler
practice.why: Requests that change data belong in POST, because browsers, crawlers and link prefetchers treat GET as safe to repeat, and a refresh can resend it. @PostMapping maps the submission, and @RequestParam reads a submitted field such as a hidden id. A GET form can't reach a POST-only mapping (Spring answers 405 Method Not Allowed), and JSON from a @RestController wouldn't render your Thymeleaf page.

practice.q: After saving a form successfully, a handler returns "redirect:/products". What happens next?
choices: Spring renders a template named redirect.html
The server forwards internally, so the browser's address bar keeps the POST URL
The browser gets a redirect and sends a new GET request for /products
Spring returns a 404, because redirect: isn't the name of any template
practice.answer: The browser gets a redirect and sends a new GET request for /products
practice.why: The redirect: prefix tells Spring to send an HTTP redirect instead of rendering a view, with the path taken relative to the application's context. The browser then requests /products with GET, which is the Post/Redirect/Get pattern, so a refresh repeats that GET instead of resubmitting the form. forward: is the server-side version that keeps the URL, and no template named redirect is involved.

practice.q: The controller runs model.addAttribute("parts", parts);. Which template markup shows one table row per part with its name?
choices: <tr th:each="p : ${parts}"><td th:text="${p.name}"></td></tr>
<tr th:for="p in parts"><td>${p.name}</td></tr>
<tr th:each="${parts}"><td th:text="name"></td></tr>
<tr th:object="${parts}"><td th:field="*{name}"></td></tr>
practice.why: th:each takes item : ${collection} and repeats its element for each item, and th:text replaces the cell's text with the expression's value. th:for only sets the HTML for attribute (as on a label) and can't loop, and a bare ${p.name} in HTML text isn't evaluated without th:text or inlining. th:each needs a loop variable, and th:text="name" would print the literal word name. th:object and th:field bind one form object to inputs; they don't loop.

practice.q: Inside a form with th:object="${part}", what does <input type="text" th:field="*{price}"/> do?
choices: It prints the price as plain text instead of an input box
It checks in the browser that price is a number before the form submits
It reads a request parameter named price from the URL
It sets the input's id, name and value and binds it to part.price
practice.answer: It sets the input's id, name and value and binds it to part.price
practice.why: th:field works with the form's th:object: *{price} means part.price, so Thymeleaf writes the input's id and name and fills its value from the current object, and on submit Spring binds the field back to the same property. Showing text is th:text's job, Bean Validation checks values on the server after the form is submitted, and reading URL parameters is what @RequestParam does in a controller.

practice.q: ProductRepository extends CrudRepository<Product, Long>. What does productRepository.findById(7L) return?
choices: A Product, or null when no row has id 7
An Optional<Product>, which is empty when no row has id 7
A List<Product> of every match
Nothing; it throws an exception right away when no row has id 7
practice.answer: An Optional<Product>, which is empty when no row has id 7
practice.why: CrudRepository's findById returns Optional<T>, empty when nothing matches, so you decide what absence means with isPresent(), orElse(...) or orElseThrow(). It doesn't return null, findAll is the method that returns many rows, and nothing is thrown until you call get() or orElseThrow() on an empty Optional.

practice.q: A library app's CommandLineRunner should add sample authors and books only when both tables are empty. Which guard matches that rule?
choices: if (authorRepo.count() == 0 || bookRepo.count() == 0)
if (authorRepo.findAll() == null)
if (authorRepo.count() == 0 && bookRepo.count() == 0)
No guard, because save() skips rows that already exist
practice.why: Both conditions must hold, so the guard needs &&. With ||, the runner seeds whenever either table is empty and duplicates the rows in the other one. findAll() returns an empty Iterable, never null, so that check is never true. save() inserts a new row for any entity without an id, so with no guard every restart adds the samples again.

practice.q: Your app seeds sample data only when its tables are empty, and spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update is set. You change spring.datasource.url from jdbc:h2:file:./shopdb to jdbc:h2:file:./shopdb2 and restart. What happens?
choices: H2 creates a new, empty shopdb2.mv.db, so the seeding runs again
H2 renames shopdb.mv.db to shopdb2.mv.db and keeps every row
Startup fails with a database-not-found error, because shopdb2.mv.db doesn't exist yet
H2 copies every row from shopdb.mv.db into the new shopdb2.mv.db file
practice.answer: H2 creates a new, empty shopdb2.mv.db, so the seeding runs again
practice.why: By default H2 creates a new database when the file named in the URL doesn't exist (adding ;IFEXISTS=TRUE to the URL would make the connection fail instead), and with ddl-auto=update Hibernate creates the tables in it, so the empty-table check passes and the samples load again. The old shopdb.mv.db stays on disk untouched, since nothing is renamed or copied. That's why renaming the file is a handy way to watch your seeding run on a clean database.

practice.q: You're writing a custom Bean Validation annotation. Which elements must it declare?
choices: value, min and max
name, type and validator
Only validatedBy, which names the validator class
message, groups and payload
practice.why: The Jakarta Validation spec requires every constraint annotation to declare message (the default error text or a key for it), groups and payload, the last two defaulting to empty. The validator class goes in the @Constraint(validatedBy = ...) meta-annotation rather than in an element of your annotation, and elements such as min or max are optional settings you add for your own rule.

practice.q: A rule says an item's stock must stay between its own minStock and maxStock fields. Where does a custom constraint for this rule belong?
choices: On the stock field, because a field validator can read the object's other fields
On the class (@Target(ElementType.TYPE)), so it can see all three fields
On the controller method, in place of @Valid
In application.properties, as a validation property
practice.answer: On the class (@Target(ElementType.TYPE)), so it can see all three fields
practice.why: A field-level validator receives only that field's value, so it can't see minStock or maxStock. A class-level constraint is placed on the type, and its isValid gets the entire object, which is how the Hibernate Validator guide checks one property against another. @Valid triggers validation but defines no rules, and properties files don't hold validation rules.

practice.q: Which handler signature lets the controller show the form again with validation messages when @Valid fails?
choices: save(BindingResult result, @Valid @ModelAttribute Item item)
save(@Valid @ModelAttribute Item item, Model model, BindingResult result)
save(@Valid @ModelAttribute Item item, BindingResult result, Model model)
save(@ModelAttribute Item item), with a try/catch block around the save call
practice.answer: save(@Valid @ModelAttribute Item item, BindingResult result, Model model)
practice.why: Spring requires the BindingResult (or Errors) parameter immediately after the validated argument. Then a failed validation fills the BindingResult, and the method can check hasErrors() and return the form view. With BindingResult first, Spring reaches it before any form object is bound and throws an IllegalStateException on every request (a 500 error), even with valid input. With Model between the two, a failed validation isn't captured and becomes a bind exception instead (a 400 by default). Without @Valid, no validation runs at all, so there's nothing to catch.

practice.q: An abstract entity Vehicle has two concrete entity subclasses and uses @Inheritance(strategy = InheritanceType.SINGLE_TABLE). Which statement is true?
choices: One table holds both subclasses' rows, plus a discriminator column
Vehicle needs its own table plus one table per subclass
Vehicle can't be an entity, because abstract classes can't be mapped
A query on Vehicle returns only rows saved as plain Vehicle objects
practice.answer: One table holds both subclasses' rows, plus a discriminator column
practice.why: SINGLE_TABLE, the default strategy, stores the whole hierarchy in one table and uses a discriminator column (DTYPE unless @DiscriminatorColumn names it) to tell the rows apart, so subclass-only columns must allow nulls. A root table plus one table per subclass is what JOINED does (TABLE_PER_CLASS gives a table only to each concrete class). An abstract class can be an entity: you never instantiate it, and a query on it returns rows of all its concrete subclasses, since no plain Vehicle can exist.

practice.q: Course has @ManyToMany Set<Student> students with a @JoinTable, and Student has @ManyToMany(mappedBy = "students") Set<Course> courses. Code adds a course only to student.getCourses() and saves the student. What happens to the join table?
choices: A new join-table row is inserted, because either side can update a many-to-many link
Nothing changes: Student is the inverse side, so add the link on Course
Hibernate throws an exception, because mappedBy makes the collection read-only
Hibernate creates a second join table for the Student side
practice.answer: Nothing changes: Student is the inverse side, so add the link on Course
practice.why: In a bidirectional relationship, the side without mappedBy owns it, and only changes on the owning side are written to the join table. Adding to the inverse collection changes the object in memory but not the database, so add the student to course.getStudents() too (keeping both sides in sync). mappedBy doesn't make anything read-only or throw; it marks the inverse side, and there's still one join table.

practice.q: A Thermostat class has setTarget(int) and getTarget(), and t is created with new Thermostat() in a @BeforeEach method, so its target starts at 0. Which JUnit test would fail if setTarget ignored its argument?
choices: @Test void target() { t.setTarget(68); }
@Test void target() { t.setTarget(68); assertNotNull(t); }
@Test void target() { t.setTarget(68); assertEquals(68, t.getTarget()); }
@Test void target() { assertEquals(t.getTarget(), t.getTarget()); }
practice.why: Only the third test checks behavior: it sets a value and asserts that the getter returns it, with the expected value first. A test without an assertion passes as long as nothing throws, assertNotNull(t) is true for any created object, and comparing the getter with itself can never fail. Using 68 rather than the starting value of 0 also lets the test tell 'stored' from 'never set'.

practice.q: You've finished a task locally and want it in the branch history that GitLab's repository graph shows. Which sequence does that?
choices: git commit -m "Add About page", then git add ., then git pull
git push, then git add ., then git commit -m "Add About page"
git add ., then git commit -m "Add About page", then git log --graph
git add ., then git commit -m "Add About page", then git push
practice.answer: git add ., then git commit -m "Add About page", then git push
practice.why: git add stages the changed files, git commit records them locally with a message, and git push uploads the new commit to the remote branch, where Code → Repository graph shows it. Committing before staging records nothing new, pushing before committing has nothing new to send, git pull only downloads, and git log --graph only draws your local history in the terminal, so a commit you don't push never reaches GitLab.

pitfalls: Missing one requirement inside a task. A single task can list several separate requirements, and a Feb 2026 student found a webinar demo that shows only one of them. Check every bullet in the running app.
Side effects you didn't test. Commenters point out that adding or updating a product can reduce part inventory. When an action should change only one record, check that nothing else moved.
Seeding on every restart. Without a guard that checks both repositories, each restart duplicates the samples, and a guard that checks only one table can still duplicate the other.
A thin commit history. One giant commit at the end, or commits that were never pushed, can't show a commit per task. Commit and push after each task with a message that names it.
A README that doesn't point anywhere. A vague note such as "updated controller" makes the evaluator hunt. Say where and what you changed, in the form your task page asks for.
Rewriting the provided design. Making Part concrete, deleting the inheritance annotations or renaming existing fields breaks forms and stored data. Add to the design instead.
Following an outdated walkthrough. Videos, the completed-project demo and older student guides may describe an earlier version of the task. When they disagree with your task page, the task page wins.
Mixing javax and jakarta. Code pasted from a Spring Boot 3 tutorial into a Spring Boot 2 project, or the reverse, fails on its imports. Match the package names your project already uses.

Validation messages that never appear. A BindingResult that doesn't come right after the @Valid parameter, a template without th:errors for that field, or a class-level message that the template never shows as a global error leaves the user with an error page or nothing at all instead of your message.
Deleting a class that's still used. Before you remove code that looks unused, such as a validator, search for references to it; an annotation left on a class breaks the build.

caveats: WGU's task page and rubric are behind the student login, so this guide describes the project only in general terms, based on student posts and comments from 2023 to 2026. 2026 reports say the project changed, so your version may differ. Your task page is the authority.
The Feb 2026 thread about the walkthroughs no longer matching is known only from a condensed summary; its link couldn't be found, so it isn't listed under community posts.

The Spring documentation cited here is for current releases (Spring Boot and Spring Data 4.2, Thymeleaf 3.1, Hibernate Validator 9.2, JUnit 6). The provided project pins its own versions in pom.xml, which may be older; if it uses Spring Boot 2, its imports are javax.*, and Spring Boot 3 or later uses jakarta.*. Follow the versions and imports already in the project.
Grading turnaround, return reasons beyond those listed and typical time to finish aren't published, and no 2026 passer's write-up was available; the plan's two weeks are a planning estimate.
Community coverage is thin: an Aug 2023 student guide with its comments and a Feb 2026 thread, neither linked here.

The practice questions are original concept checks. Where a question would otherwise hand over part of the project, it uses another domain (authors and books, a thermostat, courses and students), and none reproduces the rubric or a solution.
